summary:
We developed NOVA, an interactive lunar mission-planning platform that transforms complex space data into accessible visual insights. Planning a lunar landing is highly sensitive to time and location, as even small changes in coordinates or mission schedules can dramatically alter sunlight exposure and Earth visibility, affecting solar power and direct communications. Since existing scientific tools can be difficult for non-specialists to navigate, NOVA aims to make these changing conditions easier to understand and compare.

Using NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides and LOLA lunar elevation data, NOVA provides up to 60-day projections of terrain-aware Sun and Earth visibility for selected locations. Users can adjust coordinates, dates, mission duration, and observer height; compare candidate sites; and explore illumination hours, communication windows, periods of darkness, and upcoming horizon-crossing events. Interactive lunar visualizations help users understand why conditions change, while transparent source documentation explains the calculations and their limitations.

NOVA makes preliminary landing-site assessment faster and more understandable, helping users adapt to changing mission plans.
details:
NOVA — Making Lunar Mission Planning Accessible

Planning a lunar landing involves much more than choosing a location. Even small changes in landing coordinates or mission schedules can significantly affect sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth visibility, influencing solar power opportunities and communication planning. These challenges are particularly important near the lunar south pole, where the Sun remains close to the horizon and surrounding terrain can obstruct visibility for extended periods. Although scientific tools provide valuable data, their technical complexity can make it difficult to interpret results, compare alternatives, and adapt quickly to changing mission plans.

What We Developed

We developed NOVA, an interactive, web-based lunar mission-planning platform that transforms complex scientific data into accessible and meaningful visual insights.

Users can explore the lunar surface, select potential landing sites, adjust coordinates, choose mission dates, and customize mission duration and observer height. NOVA then produces projections of up to 60 days, estimating sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth visibility while accounting for surrounding lunar terrain.

The platform presents essential mission indicators, including total sunlight hours, Earth visibility windows, longest periods of darkness, communication gaps, and solar illumination geometry. Interactive timelines, elevation graphs, panoramic horizon views, and 3D lunar visualizations allow users to examine these conditions from multiple perspectives.

NOVA also supports exploring alternative locations and mission dates through scenario comparison, helping users understand how changing mission parameters can influence the results.

How NOVA Works

NOVA combines two main sources of scientific information: NASA/JPL SPICE ephemerides and NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data.

Using SPICE, NOVA calculates the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to an observer on the lunar surface. The calculations use DE432s planetary ephemerides and DE421 lunar orientation data, applying light-time and stellar aberration corrections within a consistent lunar reference frame.

LOLA-derived Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) provide the surrounding terrain elevations. NOVA uses these datasets to calculate the local terrain horizon, accounting for lunar curvature and potential obstructions such as ridges and crater rims.

The system evaluates terrain up to 300 kilometers from the selected location at one-degree azimuth intervals. Depending on data availability, it uses high-resolution regional terrain grids with spacing as fine as 5 meters, wider south-polar grids of 80 meters, or global elevation data.

By comparing the calculated positions of the Sun and Earth with the local terrain horizon, NOVA estimates whether either celestial body is visible at a particular time. Visibility is sampled throughout the mission, with additional refinement around detected horizon crossings.

This approach reveals not only when sunlight or direct Earth visibility is lost, but also why—whether the Sun or Earth is below the local horizon or obstructed by surrounding terrain.

Technology and Development

NOVA integrates a browser-based interactive interface, 3D lunar visualization, terrain-data processing, and a computational service for SPICE-based astronomical calculations. The platform uses NASA/JPL SPICE kernels, processed LOLA elevation models, interactive charts, and visual assets from documented sources. It is deployed as a web application using Railway, allowing users to access its analysis tools without specialized hardware.

The project also incorporates scientific data provenance, documented methodologies, and accessible explanations of its calculations, helping users distinguish between measured data, estimated results, and visual representations.

Creativity and Innovation

What makes NOVA different is its emphasis on combining scientific analysis with intuitive exploration and rapid adaptation.

Rather than presenting isolated datasets or numerical results alone, NOVA connects astronomical positions, terrain characteristics, mission timelines, and interactive visualizations within a unified experience.

Its visual approach helps users understand why conditions change. For example, a location may appear favorable based on the Sun's position, yet nearby terrain may block sunlight. NOVA makes such relationships easier to investigate through its horizon and terrain visualizations.

The platform's scenario-comparison approach also addresses a practical challenge: mission plans are rarely static. By allowing users to modify landing locations, dates, and other parameters, NOVA makes exploring alternatives more straightforward.

Educational content and interactive visual experiences further help bridge the gap between professional space-science data and public understanding of lunar environments.

Design Considerations and Scientific Reliability

Throughout development, we prioritized scientific consistency, usability, accessibility, and transparency.

We considered the effects of terrain resolution, lunar curvature, sampling intervals, observer height, coordinate systems, and the accuracy limitations of available datasets. We also made a clear distinction between visual presentation and numerical calculations.

NOVA's sunlight and Earth visibility results represent geometric line-of-sight estimates. Its solar potential indicator describes illumination geometry rather than actual electrical power generation, while Earth visibility does not guarantee a functioning radio link. Small terrain obstacles, certain short visibility windows, and other operational constraints may not be fully represented.

These limitations are documented to ensure users understand the intended scope of the results. NOVA is designed to support preliminary assessment and exploration, not replace detailed mission engineering or flight-certified systems.

Benefits and Intended Impact

NOVA aims to reduce the complexity of preliminary lunar landing-site assessment by bringing relevant information into one accessible platform.

For mission planners and researchers, it offers an intuitive way to explore how location and timing influence sunlight and communication opportunities. For students, educators, and space enthusiasts, it provides an interactive environment for understanding lunar geography, astronomical motion, and the challenges of operating on the Moon.

Ultimately, NOVA demonstrates how reliable scientific data can become more useful through thoughtful visualization and human-centered design.
